goals: Explain the features and kinds of companies, the categories of share capital and the kinds of shares
Pass journal entries for an issue of shares at par and at a premium
Record over-subscription with rejection and pro-rata allotment, and under-subscription
Explain private placement, employee stock option plans and sweat equity

slides.heading: Accounting for Share Capital
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **company**, its **share capital**, and the **issue of shares** at par and at a premium.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the company and its share capital, kinds of shares, issue at par or at a premium, over- and under-subscription, and other ways of issuing shares
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A company raises most of its capital by issuing shares to the public. In this part we learn what a company is, the kinds of share capital and shares, and how to record an issue of shares at par or at a premium. We also see what happens when the public applies for more shares, or fewer shares, than the company offers, and three other ways of issuing shares.

slides.heading: What is a company?

rows: Comes into existence on incorporation under the Companies Act 2013
Owns property, contracts, sues and is sued in its own name
A member's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on his shares
Continues to exist whatever happens to its members
Shares of a public company can be transferred freely
Shareholders own it; an elected board of directors manages it

visual.alt: Table of the features of a company: an artificial person created by law, a separate legal entity, limited liability, perpetual succession, transferable shares and separation of ownership from management

slides.narration: A company is an artificial person created by law. It is a separate legal entity, so it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name. Its members have limited liability, it continues to exist even when its members change, and the shares of a public company can be transferred freely. Ownership rests with the shareholders, while management rests with the board of directors.

slides.heading: Kinds of companies

rows: Limited by shares · limited by guarantee · unlimited
One person company (1) · private company (2 to 200) · public company (7 or more)
Government company (government holds at least 51% of paid-up capital) · non-government company
Listed company (securities on a recognised stock exchange) · unlisted company

visual.alt: Table of kinds of companies by liability, number of members, control, ownership and listing: limited by shares or guarantee or unlimited; one person, private with two to two hundred members, or public with seven or more; holding and subsidiary; government and non-government; listed and unlisted

slides.narration: Companies can be classified in several ways. By liability, a company may be limited by shares, limited by guarantee, or unlimited. By number of members, it may be a one person company, a private company with up to two hundred members, or a public company with at least seven. A government company is one in which the government holds at least fifty-one per cent of the paid-up capital.

visual.caption: Each category of capital lies within the one above it.

slides.narration: Share capital is described in layers. Authorised capital is the ceiling fixed in the memorandum. Issued capital is the part offered to the public. Subscribed capital is the part actually taken up. Called-up capital is the part the company has asked for, and paid-up capital is what it has actually received. Each layer sits inside the one above it, as the bars show.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the capital of Pragati Pumps
slides.body_md: An imagined company in Coimbatore, **Pragati Pumps Ltd**, is registered for 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It offered 1,10,000 shares; 1,00,000 were applied for and allotted. ₹8 per share has been called; a holder of 2,000 shares has not paid the last call of ₹2.
bullets: **Uncalled capital** = subscribed − called-up. **Reserve capital** is uncalled capital kept for winding up.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: authorised 20,00,000, issued 11,00,000, subscribed 10,00,000, called-up 8,00,000, uncalled 2,00,000 and paid-up 7,96,000
visual.caption: Calls in arrears: 2,000 shares × ₹2 = ₹4,000.

slides.narration: Pragati Pumps is registered for two lakh shares of ten rupees, so its authorised capital is rupees twenty lakh. It offered one lakh ten thousand shares, and one lakh were taken up. Eight rupees a share has been called, giving called-up capital of rupees eight lakh. One holder has not paid a call of rupees four thousand, so the paid-up capital is rupees seven lakh ninety-six thousand.

slides.body_md: Use the figures in the question, not those of Pragati Pumps.
slides.narration: Multiply the shares subscribed by the amount called per share. Do unpaid calls change this figure?

slides.heading: Equity shares and preference shares
bullets: Under the Companies Act 2013, preference shares must be redeemable; irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued.
columns:
**Preference shares**

- Fixed dividend, paid **first**.
- Capital repaid **before** equity on winding up.

**Equity shares**

- Dividend varies with profit.
- Full **voting rights**; bear the most risk.

rows: Only on matters affecting their rights
Higher risk, control of the company

visual.alt: Table comparing preference shares, with a fixed dividend paid first, prior repayment of capital and limited voting, and equity shares, with a varying dividend paid after preference dividend, repayment last, full voting rights, more risk and control

slides.narration: There are two kinds of shares. Preference shares carry two preferences: a dividend at a fixed rate, paid before any equity dividend, and repayment of capital before equity shareholders when the company is wound up. Equity shares carry no such preference, but their holders control the company through their voting rights and enjoy all the profits that remain.

slides.heading: Quick check: voting rights
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement is true.
slides.narration: Think about which shareholders control the company, and on what matters preference shareholders can vote.

slides.heading: How shares are issued
bullets: At **par**: at face value. At a **premium**: above face value.
At a **discount**: barred by **Section 53** (sweat equity shares are the only exception).

visual.alt: Flow of an issue of shares: a prospectus invites the public, applications arrive with application money, shares are allotted and allotment money becomes due, calls are made, and the shares become fully paid
visual.caption: Each instalment: an entry when due, an entry when received

slides.narration: A public company invites the public to buy shares through a prospectus. Investors send applications with application money. The company then allots shares and collects allotment money, and later asks for the rest through one or more calls. Shares may be issued at par, that is at face value, or at a premium. Under section fifty-three of the Companies Act, they cannot be issued at a discount, except sweat equity shares.

slides.heading: Issue at a premium: Securities Premium

headers: Securities premium may be used for (Section 52)
rows: Issuing fully paid bonus shares to members
Writing off preliminary expenses of the company
Writing off expenses of, commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures
Premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures

visual.alt: Table of the uses of securities premium under section fifty-two: bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off expenses, commission or discount on issues, premium on redemption, and buy-back; it may not be used to pay dividend or write off revenue losses
visual.caption: Only the uses are listed; bonus issue, redemption and buy-back are not accounted for in this chapter.

slides.narration: When shares are issued above face value, the excess is securities premium. It is credited to the Securities Premium Account, whichever instalment it is collected with, and shown under reserves and surplus. Section fifty-two allows it only for capital purposes, such as issuing fully paid bonus shares or writing off preliminary expenses and issue expenses. It can never be paid out as dividend.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: issue at par
slides.body_md: An imagined company in Nashik, **Godavari Agro Ltd**, issues 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on first and final call. All shares are applied for and all money is received.

Equity Share First and Final Call A/c Dr

slides.narration: Godavari Agro issues forty thousand shares at par. For each instalment, we pass one entry when the money becomes due and one when it is received. Application money of rupees eighty thousand is received and transferred to share capital. Allotment money of rupees one lakh twenty thousand, and the call of rupees two lakh, are each debited when due and credited when the cash comes in.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: issue at a premium
slides.body_md: An imagined company in Surat, **Narmada Textiles Ltd**, issues 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including premium of ₹2) and ₹4 on first and final call. The issue is fully subscribed and paid.

rows: *(Being application money on 50,000 shares transferred to share capital)*
*(Being allotment money due on 50,000 shares including premium)*
Equity Share First and Final Call A/c Dr
*(Being first and final call money due on 50,000 shares)*
To Equity Share First and Final Call A/c
*(Being first and final call money received)*

visual.alt: Journal of an imagined company issuing 50,000 shares at a premium of two rupees payable with allotment; the allotment entry credits share capital 1,50,000 and securities premium 1,00,000

slides.narration: Narmada Textiles issues fifty thousand shares of ten rupees at a premium of two rupees, payable with allotment. The allotment money due is five rupees a share, rupees two lakh fifty thousand. Of this, three rupees a share goes to share capital and two rupees a share, rupees one lakh, goes to securities premium. The premium never enters the Share Capital Account.

slides.body_md: Premium is payable with allotment.
slides.narration: Split the allotment money into its face-value part and its premium part.

slides.heading: Over-subscription: three ways to allot

rows: Allot in full to some, reject the rest
Allot pro-rata (fewer shares than applied for)
Excess application money is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the terms say so); any surplus is refunded

visual.alt: Table of ways of dealing with over-subscription: reject some applications and refund their money; allot in full to some and refund the rest; or allot pro-rata, adjusting excess application money towards allotment and refunding any surplus

slides.narration: Over-subscription means the public applies for more shares than are offered. The directors may reject some applications and refund their money, allot in full to some applicants and reject the rest, or allot on a pro-rata basis. Often they combine these. Excess application money of pro-rata allottees is usually adjusted towards their allotment money, and any surplus beyond that is refunded.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: pro-rata allotment at Narmada Textiles
slides.body_md: Same terms as worked example 3, but applications arrive for **75,000** shares. Applications for 15,000 shares are rejected; the other applicants get **5 shares for every 6 applied for**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 4: applications for 75,000 shares; 15,000 rejected and refunded 45,000; 60,000 applicants allotted 50,000 shares, five for six, with 30,000 adjusted towards allotment
visual.caption: Allotment due ₹2,50,000 − adjusted ₹30,000 = cash on allotment ₹2,20,000.

slides.narration: Suppose Narmada Textiles receives applications for seventy-five thousand shares. Applications for fifteen thousand shares are rejected, and the applicants for the other sixty thousand are allotted fifty thousand shares, five for every six. Their excess application money, rupees thirty thousand, is adjusted towards allotment, so the company collects rupees two lakh twenty thousand on allotment.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: entries for pro-rata allotment
slides.body_md: Journal entries up to the receipt of allotment money.

rows: *(Being application money on 50,000 shares transferred to share capital; excess adjusted towards allotment; money on rejected applications refunded)*
*(Being allotment money due on 50,000 shares including premium)*

visual.alt: Journal of the pro-rata allotment: application money of 2,25,000 received; transferred 1,50,000 to share capital, 30,000 to allotment and 45,000 refunded; allotment due 2,50,000 and 2,20,000 received

slides.narration: All the application money, rupees two lakh twenty-five thousand, is received first. On allotment, the Application Account is closed in three parts: rupees one lakh fifty thousand to share capital, rupees thirty thousand to the Allotment Account, and rupees forty-five thousand refunded to the rejected applicants. Then the allotment money is debited when due and credited as it is received.

slides.narration: The bar shows all the application money received. The largest part becomes share capital, at three rupees a share on the shares allotted. A smaller part is carried forward to reduce the allotment money of pro-rata applicants, and the rest is returned to the applicants who received nothing. Every rupee of application money must end up in one of these three places.

slides.narration: First find the excess application money, then subtract it from the allotment money due.

slides.heading: Under-subscription and minimum subscription

rows: Below 90%: no allotment; refund all application money

visual.alt: Table of minimum subscription: with 46,000 applications, 92 per cent, the company allots; with 44,000, 88 per cent, it must refund
visual.caption: Minimum subscription: 90% of the issue (SEBI rules), within the stipulated time.

slides.narration: Under-subscription means applications are received for fewer shares than offered. The company may allot the shares applied for, but only if it has received the minimum subscription, which is ninety per cent of the issue. A company offering fifty thousand shares could allot forty-six thousand, which is ninety-two per cent, but with only forty-four thousand applications, eighty-eight per cent, it must refund all the money.

slides.heading: Private placement, ESOP and sweat equity

rows: A select group of persons, not the public
Made through a private placement offer letter
Option to buy shares later at a price fixed now; minimum vesting period one year
For know-how or value additions; at a discount or for consideration other than cash

visual.alt: Table of other modes: private placement to a select group through an offer letter; employee stock option plan giving employees an option to buy shares later at a price fixed now; sweat equity shares to employees or directors for know-how, at a discount or for non-cash consideration

slides.narration: Besides a public issue, a company can issue shares in other ways. A private placement offers shares to a small, select group of investors rather than to the public. An employee stock option plan gives employees the right to buy shares later at a price fixed today. Sweat equity shares are given to employees or directors for their know-how or value additions, and may even be issued at a discount.

rows: Bank A/c Dr, To Share Application A/c

Share Allotment A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c, To Securities Premium A/c (if premium)
Share Call A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c

visual.alt: Summary table of entries: application money received; transferred on allotment to share capital, premium, allotment or refunded; allotment and calls debited when due and credited when received

slides.narration: To sum up: share capital moves from authorised to issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up. Each instalment is debited when due and credited when received. Premium goes to securities premium and is never used for dividend. On over-subscription, refunds and pro-rata adjustments clear the Application Account; on under-subscription, the minimum subscription decides whether shares can be allotted.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the class of share in every account: **Equity Share Capital A/c**, **Equity Share Allotment A/c**.
Show **Securities Premium** separately in the entry where the premium falls due.
In pro-rata questions, write the **working for excess application money** before the entries.
Check that the Application Account closes: capital + premium + adjusted + refunded = money received.
Shares can **never** be issued at a discount (Section 53), except sweat equity shares.
slides.narration: For the board exam, always write share capital accounts with the class of share, such as equity share capital. Show the premium separately in every entry where it falls due. In pro-rata questions, write out the working for excess application money before the entries, and check that the Application Account closes. And remember that shares can never be issued at a discount, except sweat equity shares.

slides.heading: After allotment: calls, forfeiture and disclosure
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **calls in arrears** and **in advance**, shares for **assets**, **forfeiture**, **re-issue** and the **balance sheet**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: calls in arrears and in advance, shares issued for assets, forfeiture, re-issue and disclosure in the balance sheet
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we deal with what happens after allotment. Some shareholders fail to pay calls, and some pay before the calls are made. Shares may be issued for assets instead of cash. If calls remain unpaid, the company may forfeit the shares and later re-issue them. Finally we learn how share capital is shown in the balance sheet under Schedule Three of the Companies Act.

slides.heading: Calls in arrears

headers: With a Calls in Arrears Account
rows: Bank A/c Dr, Calls in Arrears A/c Dr, To Share Call A/c
Bank A/c Dr, To Share Call A/c (cash only)
Debit balance of Calls in Arrears
Debit balance of the call account

visual.alt: Table of the two ways of recording calls in arrears: with a calls in arrears account the unpaid amount is debited to it; without one it stays as a debit balance of the call account; either way it is deducted from called-up capital
visual.caption: No interest on calls in arrears or in advance is computed in this chapter.

slides.narration: Calls in arrears are amounts called up but not paid by the due date. A company may open a Calls in Arrears Account, debiting it with the unpaid amount when the cash is recorded. Or it may simply leave the unpaid amount as a debit balance in the allotment or call account. Either way, calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital in the balance sheet. In this chapter we charge no interest on them.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: allotment at Shivalik Foods
slides.body_md: An imagined company in Dehradun, **Shivalik Foods Ltd**, issues 30,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹3 on application, ₹3 on allotment, ₹2 on first call and ₹2 on second and final call; all are applied for. **Ravi** (600 shares) pays nothing after application; **Sunita** (400 shares) pays neither call; **Kunal** (1,000 shares) pays both calls with his allotment money.

rows: *(Being application money on 30,000 shares transferred to share capital)*
*(Being allotment money received; unpaid amount debited to calls in arrears; later calls received in advance)*

visual.alt: Journal of the imagined Shivalik Foods up to allotment: allotment received with 1,800 debited to calls in arrears and 4,000 credited to calls in advance

slides.narration: Shivalik Foods, an imagined company, allots thirty thousand shares. Ravi, holding six hundred shares, does not pay his allotment money, so rupees one thousand eight hundred is debited to Calls in Arrears. Kunal, holding one thousand shares, pays both calls with his allotment, so rupees four thousand is credited to Calls in Advance. The bank receives rupees ninety-two thousand two hundred.

slides.heading: Calls in advance

visual.alt: Table of calls in advance: credited to a calls in advance account when received, transferred to the call account when the call is made, and shown under other current liabilities until then

slides.narration: Calls in advance is money received before a call is made. It is credited to a Calls in Advance Account and treated as a liability, because the company owes it to the shareholder until the call falls due. When the call is made, the advance is transferred to the call account. In the balance sheet, it is shown under other current liabilities, not as share capital.

slides.heading: Shares for consideration other than cash

nodes.label: Vendor Dr, To Share Capital, To Securities Premium

visual.alt: Flow for shares issued to a vendor: debit the assets and credit the vendor; find the number of shares by dividing the amount by the issue price; then debit the vendor and credit share capital and securities premium
visual.caption: Promoters for services: Incorporation Costs A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c

slides.narration: A company may pay for assets by issuing shares instead of cash. First the assets are debited and the vendor credited. Then the vendor is debited and share capital, along with any premium, credited. The number of shares is the amount payable divided by the issue price. slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Forfeiture check: called-up capital (+ unpaid premium) = unpaid calls + amount forfeited.
Debit **Securities Premium** on forfeiture **only** if that premium was **not received**.
Discount on re-issue **≤ amount forfeited** on those shares.
Transfer to Capital Reserve only the gain on shares **actually re-issued**.
In the note: **deduct** calls in arrears, **add** the forfeiture balance; calls in advance are a **liability**.
slides.narration: Some final advice. In forfeiture entries, check that the debits equal the credits: called-up capital, plus any unpaid premium, equals the unpaid calls plus the amount forfeited. Never let the discount on re-issue exceed the amount forfeited. Transfer to capital reserve only the gain on shares actually re-issued. And in the notes, deduct calls in arrears and add the forfeiture balance.

sections.heading: 1. The company and its kinds
sections.body_md:
A **company** is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity, limited liability of members, perpetual succession, transferable shares (public company) and separation of ownership from management.

**Kinds:** by liability (limited by shares, by guarantee, unlimited); by members (one person company; private: 2 to 200 members; public: 7 or more); by control (holding, subsidiary); by ownership (government company: at least 51% of paid-up capital held by government); listed and unlisted.

key_terms.definition_md: An artificial person created by law, having a separate legal entity and perpetual succession.
A member's liability for the company's debts is limited to the amount unpaid on his shares.
The company continues to exist whatever happens to its individual members.

sections.heading: 2. Share capital and kinds of shares
sections.body_md:
**Categories of share capital**
- **Authorised** (registered, nominal): maximum capital per the memorandum.
- **Issued:** part offered to the public. **Unissued:** the rest.
- **Subscribed:** part applied for and allotted (fully paid, or not fully paid).
- **Called-up:** part of subscribed capital asked for. **Uncalled:** the rest; **reserve capital** is uncalled capital to be called only on winding up (special resolution).
- **Paid-up** = called-up − calls in arrears.

**Kinds of shares:** **preference shares** (fixed dividend paid first; capital repaid first on winding up; limited voting; must be redeemable under the Companies Act 2013) and **equity shares** (all other shares; varying dividend; full voting rights).

key_terms.definition_md: The part of issued capital applied for by the public and allotted by the company.

A share with preference as to a fixed dividend and as to repayment of capital on winding up.

sections.heading: 4. Over-subscription and under-subscription
sections.body_md:
**Over-subscription:** applications for more shares than offered. The directors may (i) reject some applications and refund the money, (ii) allot in full to some and reject the rest, or (iii) allot **pro-rata**.

**Pro-rata allotment:** shares allotted = shares applied × allotted ÷ applied in that category. **Excess application money** = (shares applied − shares allotted) × application money per share; it is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the terms allow), and any surplus refunded.

**Transfer entry:** Share Application A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c, To Securities Premium A/c (if any), To Share Allotment A/c (adjusted), To Calls in Advance A/c (surplus kept), To Bank A/c (refunds).

**Under-subscription:** applications for fewer shares than offered; shares applied for may be allotted only if the **minimum subscription (90% of the issue)** is received; otherwise all application money is refunded.

sections.body_md:
**Calls in arrears:** amount called but unpaid. With a Calls in Arrears Account: Bank A/c Dr, Calls in Arrears A/c Dr, To Share Call A/c. **Calls in advance:** money received before a call is made. Bank A/c Dr, To Calls in Advance A/c; when the call is made, Calls in Advance A/c Dr, To Share Call A/c. Shown under **Other Current Liabilities**.

Interest on calls in arrears and in advance is not computed in this chapter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Crediting premium to Share Capital, or debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture when the premium **was** received.
- Forgetting the refund and the adjustment when closing the Application Account on over-subscription.
- Crediting Share Forfeiture with the **called-up** amount instead of the amount **received**.
- Allowing a discount on re-issue larger than the amount forfeited, or transferring the forfeiture on shares **not yet re-issued** to Capital Reserve.
- Showing calls in advance as share capital, or adding calls in arrears instead of deducting them.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: correct option, or a single concept (Section 52, minimum subscription, disclosure).
- 3 marks: categories of capital, a set of entries for one stage, a forfeiture entry, a re-issue with Capital Reserve, or a note on share capital.
- 4 marks: a full issue at a premium, pro-rata entries, a vendor purchase, or forfeiture with re-issue.
- 6 marks: a complete issue with pro-rata allotment, arrears or advance, forfeiture and re-issue, or a balance sheet with notes.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a company limited by shares?

options.text_md: It is a separate legal entity, distinct from its members
Unlimited personal liability of its members for the company's debts
Perpetual succession: it continues even when its members change
The shares of a public company are freely transferable

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Unlimited personal liability of its members for the company's debts. A member's liability is limited to the amount, if any, unpaid on his shares. The other three statements describe a company correctly.

questions.stem_md: Tunga Paper Ltd, an imagined company, is registered with 5,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It offered 3,00,000 shares to the public, received applications for 2,80,000 shares and allotted them all. So far ₹7 per share has been called up, and calls of ₹15,000 remain unpaid. Its called-up capital is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹19,60,000. Called-up capital = subscribed shares × amount called per share = 2,80,000 × ₹7 = 19,60,000. Unpaid calls reduce the paid-up capital (19,45,000), not the called-up capital.

questions.stem_md: Reserve capital of a company is

options.text_md: the part of its uncalled capital that it has resolved, by a special resolution, to call only on its winding up
the part of its authorised capital that has not yet been offered to the public
the amount of profit set aside every year as a general reserve
the amount collected as premium on the issue of shares

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the part of its uncalled capital that it has resolved, by a special resolution, to call only on its winding up. Reserve capital is uncalled capital kept back for winding up; it cannot be called while the company is a going concern. It has nothing to do with profits set aside (a revenue reserve) or with premium.

questions.stem_md: Preference shares carry a preferential right over equity shares with respect to

options.text_md: voting on every resolution placed before the shareholders
appointment of the directors of the company
payment of dividend at a fixed rate, and repayment of capital on winding up
sharing all the profits left after paying the creditors

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** payment of dividend at a fixed rate, and repayment of capital on winding up. The two preferences are a fixed dividend paid before any equity dividend and return of capital before equity shareholders on winding up. Voting control and the residual profit belong to equity shareholders.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Preference shareholders ordinarily have the same right as equity shareholders to vote on every resolution of the company.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Preference shareholders ordinarily vote only on resolutions that directly affect their own rights (and in a few special cases); equity shareholders vote on all matters.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The subscribed capital of a company can never be more than its issued capital.

**Reason (R):** Subscribed capital is the part of the issued capital that the public has applied for and the company has allotted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Shares can be allotted only out of those offered, so subscribed capital is at most the issued capital; R explains A.

questions.stem_md: Match each category of share capital in column A with its meaning in column B.

options.text_md: Authorised capital
Issued capital
Called-up capital
Reserve capital

match_right.text_md: The part of authorised capital offered to the public for subscription
The part of uncalled capital to be called only on winding up
The maximum capital a company may raise, as stated in its memorandum
The part of subscribed capital that shareholders have been asked to pay

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The categories nest inside one another: authorised, then issued, then subscribed, then called-up, then paid-up; reserve capital is a part of the uncalled amount.

questions.stem_md: The maximum amount of share capital that a company may raise, as stated in its memorandum of association, is called its ___ capital.
questions.solution_md: It is the authorised (also called nominal or registered) capital.

It offered 2,40,000 shares to the public, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment, ₹3 on first call and ₹2 on final call. Applications were received for 2,25,000 shares, and all were allotted. The final call has not yet been made. A shareholder holding 4,000 shares did not pay the first call. Calculate the authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up, uncalled and paid-up capital.
questions.solution_md: Each category is a number of shares times an amount per share; only paid-up capital deducts the unpaid calls.

questions.solution_md: Any three bases, each with both columns correct, earn the marks.

questions.stem_md: Shares are issued at a premium and the premium is payable with the allotment money. The entry for the allotment money becoming due is

options.text_md: Share Allotment A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c only
Securities Premium A/c Dr, To Share Allotment A/c
Share Allotment A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c and To Securities Premium A/c
Bank A/c Dr, To Securities Premium A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Share Allotment A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c and To Securities Premium A/c. The amount due on allotment is debited to Share Allotment; the face-value part is credited to Share Capital and the premium part to Securities Premium. Cash is recorded only when it is received.

questions.stem_md: Under Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013, the balance of the Securities Premium Account can NOT be used for

options.text_md: paying a dividend to the shareholders
writing off the preliminary expenses of the company
writing off the expenses of, or commission paid on, an issue of shares or debentures
issuing fully paid bonus shares to the members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** paying a dividend to the shareholders. Securities premium is a capital receipt, so the Act lists only capital uses for it; it may never be distributed as dividend.

questions.stem_md: Under Section 53 of the Companies Act 2013, an issue of shares at a discount (other than sweat equity shares) is

options.text_md: permitted if the discount does not exceed 10 per cent of the face value
permitted with the approval of the board of directors alone
permitted if the discount is credited to the Securities Premium Account
not permitted; any shares so issued are void

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** not permitted; any shares so issued are void. Section 53 bars a company from issuing shares at a discount, the only exception being sweat equity shares issued under Section 54.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company offers 1,00,000 shares to the public and, by the closing date, receives applications for only 85,000 shares. Applying the minimum subscription rule of 90 per cent of the issue, the company must

options.text_md: allot 85,000 shares and treat the issue as under-subscribed
refund the application money; no shares can be allotted
allot 1,00,000 shares and ask the directors to pay for the shortfall
allot 85,000 shares and offer the rest at a discount

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** refund the application money; no shares can be allotted. Applications cover only 85% of the issue, which is below the minimum subscription of 90%. So no allotment can be made and the money received must be refunded.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An issue is said to be under-subscribed when the company receives applications for fewer shares than it has offered.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** That is the meaning of under-subscription; the company may still allot the shares applied for, provided the minimum subscription has been received.

questions.stem_md: Kosi Polymers Ltd, an imagined company, offered 60,000 shares of ₹10 each, ₹4 payable on application. Applications were received for 56,000 shares, and all of them were allotted. The amount credited to Share Capital on transfer of the application money is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹2,24,000. Only the shares actually allotted count: 56,000 × ₹4 = 2,24,000. The issue is under-subscribed but above the 90% minimum, so the allotment is valid.

questions.stem_md: Arpita applied for 1,800 shares in an imagined company and was allotted 1,200 shares on a pro-rata basis. Application money was ₹4 and allotment money ₹3 per share, and her excess application money was to be adjusted towards allotment. The amount adjusted towards allotment is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹2,400. Excess = (1,800 − 1,200) × ₹4 = 2,400. Allotment due from her is 3,600, which is more than the excess, so the whole 2,400 is adjusted.

questions.stem_md: Varuna Marine Ltd, an imagined company, offered 40,000 shares, with ₹3 per share payable on application. Applications for 52,000 shares were received; applications for 12,000 shares were rejected and the remaining applicants were allotted shares in full. The application money refunded is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹36,000. Only the rejected applicants get their money back: 12,000 × ₹3 = 36,000. The rest is transferred to share capital.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company issued shares of ₹10 each: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment and ₹3 on first and final call. Bhavna applied for 900 shares and was allotted 600 shares on a pro-rata basis; her excess application money is adjusted towards allotment. How much must she pay on allotment (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Excess application money = (900 − 600) × ₹3 = 900. Allotment due = 600 × ₹4 = 2,400. Amount payable = 2,400 − 900 = 1,500. So ₹1,500.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company issued 25,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹3 per share. The issue was fully subscribed and all the money was received. What is the balance of its Securities Premium Account (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Securities premium = 25,000 × ₹3 = 75,000. So ₹75,000.

questions.stem_md: The premium received on the issue of shares is credited to the ___ Account.
questions.solution_md: It is credited to the Securities Premium Account, which appears under Reserves and Surplus.

**Reason (R):** Securities premium may be used to pay dividend to the shareholders.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: Section 52 allows only capital uses of securities premium, and dividend is not one of them.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When shares are allotted on a pro-rata basis, the excess application money of an allottee may be adjusted towards the allotment money due from him.

**Reason (R):** An allottee who receives fewer shares than he applied for has paid more application money than is due on the shares allotted to him.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: it is precisely because he has overpaid on application that the company can use the excess against his allotment.

questions.solution_md: One mark for each correct meaning.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Private placement:** an offer of shares by a company to a select group of persons (such as institutions or chosen investors), not to the public at large, through a private placement offer letter (Section 42 of the Companies Act 2013).
2. **Employee Stock Option Plan:** an option given to the employees and whole-time directors of a company to buy its shares at a future date at a predetermined price, usually lower than the market price; employees may or may not exercise it after the vesting period.
3. **Sweat equity shares:** shares issued by a company to its employees or directors at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how, intellectual property rights or value additions (Section 54).
